title: Valley Berry curvature dipole induced nonlinear valley Hall effect
authors: Lulu Xiong, Xue-Jin Zhang, Zeying Zhang, Yinning Zhou, Jin Cao, Cong Xiao, Shengyuan A. Yang
abstract: Valley Hall effect is a signature effect in the field of valleytronics, and recent studies have pushed this effect into the nonlinear regime. Here, we reveal a previously unexplored type of nonlinear valley Hall effect which arises from a valley Berry curvature dipole (vBCD) mechanism. We show this nonlinear valley Hall effect is forbidden for conventional time-reversal-connected valleys, but is supported in the class of valleytronic systems featuring time-reversal-invariant valleys. The candidate layer groups and detailed symmetry constraints on vBCD are obtained. It shows the nonlinear valley Hall response, as well as the nonlinear charge Hall response, can be well controlled by tuning the driving field direction. We demonstrate our proposal in an effective model study and in a concrete material example, strained Nb$_{3}$SBr$_{7}$, by first-principles calculations. The nonlocal transport signature of this vBCD induced nonlinear valley Hall effect is also discussed.
summary: This work introduces a novel nonlinear valley Hall effect driven by the valley Berry curvature dipole (vBCD) in materials with time-reversal-invariant valleys (TRIVs). The authors theoretically prove this effect is symmetry-protected and demonstrate its feasibility using first-principles calculations on strained $	ext{Nb}_3	ext{SBr}_7$. It provides a pathway for controlling valley-specific transport responses in 2D materials.
main_problem: The paper investigates a previously unexplored nonlinear valley Hall effect (VHE) mechanism driven by the valley Berry curvature dipole (vBCD). It specifically focuses on systems where valleys are related by crystal symmetry rather than time-reversal symmetry.
main_result: The vBCD-induced nonlinear VHE is forbidden in conventional time-reversal-connected valleys but is supported in time-reversal-invariant valley (TRIV) systems. The effect allows for selective control between valley and charge Hall responses.
method: The study combines theoretical symmetry analysis (searching 80 layer groups) with first-principles calculations on a concrete material example ($	ext{Nb}_3	ext{SBr}_7$) and proposes nonlocal transport measurements.
model_or_system: The system under study is a 2D nonmagnetic material exhibiting two valleys ($	ext{V}_1, 	ext{V}_2$) in the conduction band, specifically focusing on TRIV systems. The analysis uses symmetry groups and effective models derived from $k \cdot p$ theory.
key_observables: Nonlinear VHE current ($j_v$), nonlinear charge Hall response, and nonlocal voltage signals ($	ext{V}_{3\omega}^{	ext{NL}} \propto ho^3$, $	ext{V}_{4\omega}^{	ext{NL}} \propto ho^4$).
important_parameters: Relaxation time ($	au$), the valley Berry curvature dipole ($\Lambda_v$), and the driving electric field direction relative to $\Lambda_v$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the Fermi level is near the band edge and focuses on the two relevant valleys. The vBCD mechanism is necessary but not sufficient for the effect.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the vBCD mechanism in TRIV systems and show the dependence of the nonlinear VHE conductivity ($\chi_v$) on the angle between the driving field and $\Lambda_v$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem, develops the theoretical framework using symmetry constraints to identify candidate materials, derives the nonlinear transport equations, and validates the predictions using both model calculations and a concrete material example ($	ext{Nb}_3	ext{SBr}_7$).
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter transport, the concept of Berry curvature dipoles and nonlinear responses relates to geometric phases and topological invariants, which are key concepts in advanced quantum physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of a valleytronic system with two valleys V1 and V2. For a TRIV system, the two valleys are connected by some crystal symmetry Q, rather than by time-reversal symmetry T .

FIG. 2. Schematic illustration of vBCD and the induced non- linear VHE. (a) At each individual valley, the valley-resolved BCD (ΛV1 and ΛV2) arises from the asymmetric distribution of Berry curvature. (b) The valley-contrasting component of ΛV1 and ΛV2 gives rise to the vBCD. When an electric field is applied along the vBCD direction, a nonlinear valley Hall current jv is produced in the transverse direction.

FIG. 4. (a) Illustration of a hexagonal crystal having three C3z- connected valleys at the three M points. (b) Under a uniaxial strain, the hexagonal lattice becomes a centered rectangular lattice. And the energy degeneracy among the three M valleys is lifted, resulting in a pair of TRIVs.

FIG. 3. Exhibition of vBCD and the induced nonlinear VHE in an effective model of LG 13. (a,b) The Berry curvature distributions of V1 and V2 valleys on the Fermi surface. The dashed lines represent the Fermi surfaces at a chemical po- tential of µ = 0.2 eV. The arrows indicate the direction of valley-resolved BCD. (c) The x- and y-components of vBCD as functions of chemical potential. (d) The calculated nonlin- ear valley Hall conductivity as a function of the direction of electric field.
FIG. 5. (a,b) Top and side views of monolayer Nb3SBr7. The mirror line associated with the Mx symmetry is shown by the dashed line. (c) Calculated band structure of the unstrained monolayer Nb3SBr7.
